BLM’s Motion for Summary Judgment Granted;
WildLands Defense’s Appeals Dismissed
I. Summary
WildLands Defense (WLD) has appealed 17 Final Decisions dated February
28, 2020, and issued by the Field Manager of the Jarbidge Field Office (JFO), Bureau
of Land Management (BLM). The Final Decisions renew, with modifications, the
grazing permits for numerous grazers holding permits for grazing allotments within
the Devil Creek subregion of the JFO’s jurisdiction.
Now pending and fully briefed are cross-motions for summary judgment
filed by WLD and BLM. Also pending are cross-motions for summary judgment
regarding appeals of the Final Decisions filed by Western Watersheds Project
(WWP) and grazers, but those motions are addressed in separate Orders.
11

ID-JFO-2020-001 through -034
Historically, the Devil Creek subregion was vegetated with sage-
shrub/bunchgrass vegetation communities. Currently, its vegetation is primarily
non-native grasslands, the chief causal factors being repeated wildfires and post-fire
seedings with crested wheatgrass and Siberian wheatgrass. In addition, non-native
annual grasses such as cheatgrass, are common, providing fine fuels that exacerbate
wildfire spread.
Drawing from the management outlined in the 2015 Jarbidge Resource
Management Plan (2015 RMP), the BLM elected to manage livestock grazing in the
subregion to reduce fine fuels and create openings for extant shrub communities to
expand. Therefore, the Final Decisions increase grazing levels, sometimes
substantially, to in turn increase utilization levels and expand livestock distribution
to better reduce non-native plant species. This, coupled with vegetation treatments
to restore vegetative resilience, are the means BLM outlined in its 2015 RMP to
improve rangeland conditions over the life of the RMP.
In a single Statement of Reasons (SOR) for appeal of all the Final Decisions,
WLD asserts that BLM’s management reflected in the Final Decisions will lead to
further degradation of an already degraded landscape. It argues the only avenue to
improve conditions is to significantly reduce grazing levels; remove infrastructure
such as fences, pipelines and troughs; and re-introduce native plant species. WLD
also alleges that BLM failed to comply with the National Environmental Policy Act
(NEPA), Federal Land Policy and Management Act (FLPMA), and grazing
regulations.
However, WLD—which has the burden of demonstrating that BLM’s Final
Decisions lack a rational basis or that BLM has not substantially complied with the
law—has failed to adduce specific facts showing that there is a genuine issue of
material fact or that legally, BLM is not entitled to judgment. Therefore, BLM’s
motion for summary judgment must be granted, WLD’s motion for summary
judgment is denied, and WLD’s appeals are dismissed.
II. General Background
Within the area under the jurisdiction of the JFO (JFO Area) are 1.7 million
acres of public and private lands in southcentral Idaho, including 93 grazing
allotments. The area includes 911,000 acres of habitat for sage-grouse, a BLM special
status species, 600,000 acres of which has been burned by wildfire in recent years.
12

ID-JFO-2020-001 through -034
With respect to the 357,816-acre Devil Creek subregion, wildfire is the
primary factor influencing vegetation composition and wildlife habitats in the
subregion. Between 1993 and 2013, approximately 284,160 acres (80 percent) of
BLM-managed lands in the subregion burned at least once. Of the total burned area,
approximately half (141,390 acres) burned more than once. Wildfire activity was
particularly large in scope during the period of 2007 through 2012, when the
Murphy Complex Fire and other large fires burned over 800,000 acres within the
JFO Area, including 403,560 acres within the Devil Creek subregion (some areas
burned more than once).
Much of the subregion was historically populated with sagebrush steppe
plant communities. The subregion is currently dominated by herbaceous vegetation
largely as the result of past fire, due to either post-fire grass and forb seeding or
natural recovery of native or seeded species.
Grazing management in the JFO Area is the product of over 15 years of
litigation between WWP, grazing permittees, and the BLM. In a 2005 settlement
addressing that litigation, the BLM agreed to (1) undertake a revision of the 1987
Jarbidge Rangeland Management Plan (RMP); (2) fully process new permits for all
allotments in the JFO Area with new environmental analyses to address the impact
of grazing and associated infrastructure; and (3) implement grazing management as
described in the settlement agreement in the interim between the approval of the
settlement agreement and the issuance of final grazing decisions. See Final Decision1
at 2 (e.g., BER 042772) (summarizing the litigation).
In September 2015, BLM issued its record of decision for the Jarbidge RMP,
which was amended a week later by the multi-state Approved Resource
Management Plan Amendments for Sage-grouse (2015 ARMPA). Vegetation is the
driving focus of the 2015 RMP. Management under the plan is directed at shifting
vegetative communities from native and non-native perennial (such as crested
wheatgrass and Siberian wheatgrass) grasslands and annual grasses (such as
cheatgrass) towards shrublands with perennial grass understories. One way to do
so is for BLM to take interim steps to reduce fine fuels and open spaces in dense
grassland communities to allow sagebrush to spread.

13

ID-JFO-2020-001 through -034
Thus, in the 2015 RMP, BLM increased its livestock allocation from
approximately 189,000 animal unit months (AUMs) in the 1987 RMP to up to
approximately 326,000 AUMs in the 2015 RMP. This was done in response to data
showing large quantities of forage available for livestock under the vegetation
allocations, and low levels of utilization. Grazing levels are expected to decline over
the life of the plan, as shrub-dominated vegetative communities expand.
BLM and the U.S. Forest Service developed the 2015 ARMPA in response to
the 2010 finding of the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) under the Endangered
Species Act that listing Greater sage-grouse (sage-grouse) was warranted but
precluded for listing due to higher agency priorities. 75 Fed. Reg. 13910 (March 23,
2010). Sagebrush habitat—which is critically important to sage-grouse, a sagebrush
obligate—and sage-grouse populations have experienced serious long-term and
short-term declines throughout the sage-grouse’s range, including the Devil Creek
subregion and the rest of the JFO Area. One of the ARMPA’s goals is to conserve,
enhance, and restore the sagebrush ecosystem upon which the sage-grouse
populations depend in an effort to maintain and/or increase their abundance and
distribution.
The 2015 ARMPA established a three-tier management system for sage-
grouse habitat based on the most important habitat across the species’ range: (1)
priority habitat management areas (PHMA), which are identified as having the
highest habitat value for maintaining sustainable sage-grouse populations; (2)
important habitat management areas (IHMA), which provide a management buffer
for and connect patches of PHMA; and (3) general habitat areas (GHMA), which are
occupied seasonally or year-round outside of PHMAs. The management areas are
based on the State of Idaho’s key habitat maps, which identify areas necessary for
sage-grouse conservation. 2015 Record of Decision and ARMPAs for the Great Basin
Sub-Regions at 2-9 (BER 010710) and 2-10 (BER 010711). Under the ARMPA, 80
percent of JFO-managed lands in the Devil Creek subregion are mapped as sage-
grouse habitat, with 17 percent being Priority Habitat Management Areas (PHMA),
50 percent being Important Habitat Management Areas (IHMA), and 23 percent
being General Habitat Management Areas (GHMA).
Currently, because population triggers included in the 2015 ARMPA have
been tripped; lands designated IHMA are managed as if they were PHMA.
However, because grazing management actions associated with PHMA are no

ID-JFO-2020-001 through -034
different than management actions under IHMA, none of the actions approved in
the challenged decisions are affected. Id.
In 2016, the JFO undertook to fully process new grazing permits by dividing
the 1.7 million-acre JFO Area into subregions based on similar geographic
characteristics and resource issues. The Devil Creek subregion is the first subregion
to be analyzed by the JFO.
As part of the JFO’s permit renewal process for the subregion, a BLM
interdisciplinary team (ID Team) prepared Rangeland Health Assessments and
Evaluations (RHA) to determine whether grazing allotments and pastures were
meeting the Idaho Standards for Rangeland Health (Standards). As part of this
process, the JFO collected field data and requested relevant information from
grazing permittees and interested publics to include in the RHA.
The Standards are: 1 (Watersheds), 2 (Riparian Areas and Wetlands), 3
(Stream Channels and Floodplains), 4 (Native Plant Communities), 5 (Seedings), 6
(Exotic Plant Communities, Other than Seedings), 7 (Water Quality), and 8
(Threatened and Endangered Plants and Animals). Not all the Standards apply to
all the allotments. The following table shows the number of allotments in the
subregion to which each Standard applies, the number of allotments meeting or
making significant progress in meeting each Standard (M or MP), and the number of
allotments not meeting each Standard (NM).

Lack of sagebrush cover is a primary reason for many of the allotments failing
to meet Standards 1, 4, 5, and 8. Historic livestock grazing was a contributing causal
factor in many instances and current livestock grazing was a contributing causal
factor in few allotments.
For most of the allotments not meeting one or more of the Standards which
apply to water resources and wetlands, i.e., Standards 2, 3, and/or 7, water
diversions and altered streamflow associated with upstream private land use is the
causal factor for not meeting the Standard(s). Only three allotments (Grassy Hills,
15

ID-JFO-2020-001 through -034
Cedar Creek Canyon, and Pigtail Butte) contain pastures that are not meeting one or
more of those Standards because of current livestock grazing management practices.
The JFO then prepared an environmental assessment (EA) that focused on
addressing livestock grazing impacts on public land resources. In the EA, the JFO
considered a total of nine alternatives and analyzed the following six alternatives in
detail:
• Alternative 1 – Current Management: Alternative 1 would carry forward all
allotment management, including average AUMs, livestock numbers, seasons
of use, grazing systems, terms and conditions, and monitoring, that has
occurred in the allotments over the past 10 years. No new range
infrastructure is proposed under this alternative.
• Alternative 2 – Permittee Proposed Action: Alternative 2 is the permittee’s
proposal and includes AUMs, season of use, management strategies, new or
modified range infrastructure, and allotment or pasture boundary
adjustments, as applied for by the current grazing permit holder. This
alternative includes range infrastructure projects whose construction would
disturb about 585 acres.
• Alternative 3 – Vegetative Production: Alternative 3 is based on the most
current vegetative production data and the method used for forage allocation
in the 2015 RMP (see Appendix D of the EA). Alternative 3 also includes
adaptive management in the form of Objectives, Management Guidelines,
Thresholds, Grazing Systems, and Monitoring assigned to each pasture and a
Response Toolbox if Management Guidelines or Thresholds are exceeded (see
Appendix E of the EA), as well as new and modified range infrastructure.
The grazing schedule—in terms of seasons of use, classes of livestock,
livestock numbers, and pasture rotations—would be determined annually
prior to the start of the grazing season in coordination with the permittee and
based on a review of applicable monitoring data. Livestock grazing
management would be consistent with the terms and conditions, as well as,
the Objectives, Management Guidelines, Thresholds, and Grazing Systems
assigned to each pasture. This alternative includes range infrastructure
projects whose construction would disturb about 575 acres.
• Alternative 4 – Forage Availability and Resource Needs: Alternative 4
incorporates the vegetative production allocations as defined above for
16

ID-JFO-2020-001 through -034
Alternative 3 but adjusts AUMs for slope, distance to water, sage-grouse
breeding and nesting habitats, and other resource concerns (see Appendix D
of the EA). Alternative 4 also includes adaptive management in the form of
Objectives, Management Guidelines, Thresholds, Grazing Systems, and
Monitoring assigned to each pasture and a Response Toolbox if Management
Guidelines or Thresholds are exceeded (see Appendix E of the EA), as well as
new and modified range infrastructure. The grazing schedule, in terms of
seasons of use, classes of livestock, livestock numbers, and pasture rotations
would be determined annually prior to the start of the grazing season in
coordination with the permittee and based on a review of applicable
monitoring data. Livestock grazing management would be consistent with
the terms and conditions, as well as the Objectives, Management Guidelines,
Thresholds, and Grazing Systems assigned to each pasture. This alternative
includes range infrastructure projects whose construction would disturb
about 437 acres.
• Alternative 5 – Reduced Grazing: Alternative 5 reduces the AUMs and
livestock numbers from Alternative 1 (Current Management) by half. Season
of use and monitoring would be the same as those described for Alternative
1. No new range infrastructure is proposed under this alternative.
• Alternative 6 – No Grazing: Under Alternative 6, no livestock grazing would
be authorized on public lands within the allotment for a term of 10 years.
For the adaptive management in Alternatives 3 and 4, the Management
Guidelines and Thresholds outline the grazing management expected to meet the
Objective(s) for each pasture. Grazing will be adjusted if BLM determines that
management is not supporting the Objectives and Management Guidelines.
The intent of the Management Guidelines is to achieve, or make progress
towards achieving, the Objective(s). Thresholds are intended to ensure that
livestock grazing management is consistent with Objectives and Management
Guidelines. Together, the Objectives, Management Guidelines, Thresholds, and
Responses manage livestock grazing to meet objectives in the 2015 RMP and to
meet, or make significant progress towards meeting, the Standards, where progress
can be made using grazing management alone.
The management outlined by the Objectives and Management Guidelines is
expected to maintain perennial plant species, protect soils, and reduce the likelihood
17

ID-JFO-2020-001 through -034
of wildfire spread to habitat for native and special status species, in the event of
ignition. Pastures will be managed to achieve utilization levels at or below the
assigned Management Guidelines.
To achieve this, use supervision/compliance monitoring will be conducted
periodically during the grazing season and end use monitoring will occur after

A. Standards for Summary Judgment and Burden of Proof
Although the regulations do not specifically authorize motions for summary
judgment, the Interior Board of Land Appeals (IBLA) has long recognized the

procedure as an appropriate means for resolving issues without a hearing. Larson v.
BLM, 129 IBLA 250, 252 (1994); Stamatakis v. BLM, 115 IBLA 69, 74 (1990). Federal
courts provide that a party is entitled to summary judgment if there are no genuine
issues of material fact and, as a matter of law, summary judgment is appropriate.
Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317, 322-23 (1986) (construing Rule 56 of the Federal
Rules of Civil Procedure).
In considering this question, this Tribunal must view the record evidence in
the light most favorable to the non-moving party, drawing all reasonable inferences
in its favor. Dannelle and Chad Hensley, et al., 195 IBLA 345, 354 (2020). Because WLD
has the ultimate substantive burden of proof in a challenge to BLM grazing
decisions, id. at 346, BLM, as the moving party on its summary judgment motion,
need only point out that there is an absence of evidence to support the case of WLD,
the nonmoving party. Celotex Corp., 477 U.S. at 323.
Once the moving party has met its burden, the burden then shifts to the non-
moving party to set forth by affidavit, or other means, specific facts showing that
there is a genuine issue of material fact or that legally, the moving party is not
entitled to judgment. T. W. Elec. Serv. Inc. v. Pac. Elec. Contractors Ass’n, 809 F.2d 626,
630 (9th Cir. 1987). Legal memoranda are not evidence and do not create issues of
fact capable of defeating an otherwise valid motion for summary judgment. British
Airways Bd. V. Boeing Co., 585 F2d 946, 952 (9th Cir. 1978).
Although Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 56, the Federal
summary judgment rule, does not apply to the Board or the
Departmental Cases Hearings Division, statements of the burden of
proof by Federal courts applying that rule serve as useful guidance to
the Board and ALJs. For example, the Supreme Court has explained
that appellants attempting to satisfy their burden to identify genuine
issues of material fact must set forth specific facts showing the
existence of such an issue and may not simply rest on mere allegations
or denials “without ‘any significant probative evidence tending to
support’” their claims. Evidence that is “merely colorable” or “not
significantly probative” is insufficient to defeat summary judgment.
. . . A “material” fact is one which “might affect the outcome of the suit
